source_passage: The windmill had ceased to exist! At this sight the animals’ courage returned to them. The fear and despair they had felt a moment earlier were drowned in their rage against this vile, contemptible act. A mighty cry for vengeance went up, and without waiting for further orders they charged forth in a body and made straight for the enemy. This time they did not heed the cruel pellets that swept over them like hail. It was a savage, bitter battle. The men fired again and again, and, when the animals got to close quarters, lashed out with their sticks and their heavy boots. A cow, three sheep, and two geese were killed, and nearly everyone was wounded. Even Napoleon, who was directing operations from the rear, had the tip of his tail chipped by a pellet. source_passage: Then Snowball (for it was Snowball who was best at writing) took a brush between the two knuckles of his trotter, painted out MANOR FARM from the top bar of the gate and in its place painted ANIMAL FARM. This was to be the name of the farm from now onwards. After this they went back to the farm buildings, where Snowball and Napoleon sent for a ladder which they caused to be set against the end wall of the big barn. They explained that by their studies of the past three months the pigs had succeeded in reducing the principles of Animalism to Seven Commandments. These Seven Commandments would now be inscribed on the wall; they would form an unalterable law by which all the animals on Animal Farm must live for ever after.
interpretation: In this passage, Snowball’s act of renaming Manor Farm to Animal Farm symbolizes a significant shift from human oppression to self-governance among the animals. The change in name is not merely cosmetic but reflects an ideological transformation and rejection of their previous servitude under the farm's human owner. The inscription of the Seven Commandments on the wall represents the establishment of a new set of immutable laws, which are intended to govern all animals equally, embodying the ideals of equality and autonomy. However, this moment also introduces the theme of ideological control, as these commandments will serve as the foundation for a regime that may be prone to corruption, setting up future conflicts over their interpretation and enforcement.

source_passage: At first they pretended to laugh to scorn the idea of animals managing a farm for themselves. The whole thing would be over in a fortnight, they said. They put it about that the animals on the Manor Farm (they insisted on calling it the Manor Farm; they would not tolerate the name “Animal Farm”) were perpetually fighting among themselves and were also rapidly starving to death. When time passed and the animals had evidently not starved to death, Frederick and Pilkington changed their tune and began to talk of the terrible wickedness that now flourished on Animal Farm. It was given out that the animals there practised cannibalism, tortured one another with red-hot horseshoes, and had their females in common. This was what came of rebelling against the laws of Nature, Frederick and Pilkington said. However, these stories were never fully believed.
interpretation: This passage from a dystopian novel reflects the theme of propaganda and misinformation employed by adversaries to undermine the achievements of others. The characters Frederick and Pilkington initially ridicule the idea that animals can manage their own affairs but, upon realizing their persistence, they shift tactics to spread rumors about internal strife, starvation, and moral degradation at the farm managed by the animals. This change in strategy underscores how those who fear being displaced or outshone seek to discredit their rivals through false narratives. The fact that these claims are never fully believed highlights a broader theme of public skepticism towards disinformation campaigns, suggesting an underlying awareness of reality amidst the chaos and deceit.

I was in a state of temporary death. This state was known to the

ancients, but as far as I am informed it is unknown to us. I have

no conception of how long I was dead, probably not longer than five

or ten seconds, but after awhile I arose from the dead and opened

my eyes. But I felt I was falling down--down--down. I

stretched out my hand to attach myself to something but the rough

wall scratched my fingers; it was running away from me, upward. I

felt blood on my fingers. It was clear that all this was not merely

a play of my sick imagination. I heard my own frequent, trembling breaths. (I am not ashamed to

confess this, it was all unexpected and incomprehensible.) A minute,

two, three passed; I was still going down.
interpretation: This passage from a dystopian novel employs vivid imagery and metaphor to convey a sense of existential crisis and disorientation. The protagonist's "temporary death" symbolizes an extreme psychological or physical state where reality is distorted, suggesting a breakdown of the usual boundaries between life and death, consciousness and unconsciousness. The downward motion described represents a descent into chaos or despair, reflecting themes of helplessness and loss of control in a dystopian society that may be indifferent to human suffering. The wall moving upward away from the protagonist underscores their isolation and alienation, emphasizing the novel's critique of societal detachment and the erosion of personal stability within oppressive conditions.

This is that

divine justice of which those stone-housed ancients dreamed, lit by

the naive pink rays of the dawn of history. Their "God" punished

sacrilege as a capital crime. You Uranians, morose and as black as the ancient Spaniards, who

were wise in knowing so well how to burn at the stake, you are

silent; I think you agree with me. But I hear you, pink Venerians,

saying something about "tortures, executions, return to barbarism."

My dear Venerians, I pity you! You are incapable of philosophical,

mathematical thinking. Human history moves upward in circles,

like an aero. The circles are at times golden, sometimes they are

bloody, but all have 360 degrees. They go from 0° to 10°, 20°, 200°,

360°,--and then again 0°. Yes, we have returned to zero.
interpretation: This passage reflects on the cyclical nature of human history and societal justice within a dystopian framework. The narrator contrasts the divine retributions and barbaric practices of ancient civilizations with contemporary forms of punishment, suggesting that while methods may evolve, the essence of enforcing moral order remains unchanged. By likening historical progression to an upward spiral with both golden and bloody phases, the author critiques the notion of linear progress in human civilization, arguing instead for a repetitive cycle where societies return to foundational principles of justice and retribution, albeit in different forms. This cyclical view underscores themes of existential pessimism and the futility of striving for perfect societal advancement, implying that humanity is bound by recurring patterns of violence and moral judgment.

And I see how there in the height, in the

purest rarified air, my judgment about the only "right" bursts with

a crack, like a pneumatic tire. I see clearly that only an atavism,

the absurd superstition of the ancients, gives me this idea of

"right."



There are ideas of clay and ideas moulded of gold, or of our

precious glass. In order to know the material of which an idea is

made, one needs only to let fall upon it a drop of strong acid. One of these acids was known to the ancients under the name of

_reductio ad absurdum_. This was the name of it, I think. But they

were afraid of this poison; they preferred to believe that they saw

_heaven_, even though it was a toy made of clay, rather than confess

to themselves that it was only a blue nothing.
interpretation: The passage critiques rigid adherence to outdated or irrational beliefs by presenting them as illusions comparable to fragile objects made of clay. The author uses imagery such as "pneumatic tire" and "drop of strong acid" to illustrate the fragility of conventional notions of rightness that are based on superstition rather than reason or reality. This critique underscores themes of skepticism towards traditional authority, the importance of critical thinking, and the potential for enlightenment through challenging established beliefs, even when those beliefs are deeply held and comforting. The reference to ancient fear of reductio ad absurdum highlights how societies can prefer comfortable delusions to unsettling truths, a warning against intellectual complacency in the face of complex realities.
